title: India's Jet Fuel Stabilisation Fund Just Went Live. Airlines Are Not Signing Up.
excerpt: The ₹10,000 crore aviation fuel fund fixes ATF at ₹115 per litre for three years. But a 10% price hike today and a three-year lock-in have carriers hesitating.
body:
India's ₹10,000 crore ($1.05 billion) Aviation Turbine Fuel Price Stabilisation Fund is now operational. Aviation turbine fuel will be sold to domestic airlines at a fixed rate of ₹115 per litre under the scheme — and that is the first problem.

The fixed price is 10% higher than what airlines were paying before the scheme launched.

Indian airlines have so far not opted in, according to industry sources. The scheme's design explains why: carriers that join are locked into the ₹115 rate for up to three years, even if global fuel prices decline. The excess payments would be used to replenish the fund, not returned to the airlines. Airlines that stay out continue paying market-linked prices, which are currently higher but could fall.

It is, in effect, a bet on permanently elevated fuel costs. And no airline wants to make that bet right now.

**The economics of aviation fuel in India.** ATF accounts for up to 40% of an Indian airline's operating costs — among the highest ratios in the world. That share has been climbing since the Iran war began on February 28, pushing global oil prices from roughly $75 per barrel to nearly $120 before settling around $97.

India's ATF prices jumped in lockstep. What was already one of the most expensive fuel markets for airlines — thanks to decades of state and central taxes layered on top of global prices — became nearly unbearable.

The fund was the government's answer. Union Cabinet approved it earlier this month, framing it as a temporary stabilisation mechanism rather than a subsidy. The money will flow as interest-free advances to oil marketing companies — Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum, Hindustan Petroleum — to cover the gap between market prices and the capped rate.

**But the devil is in the lock-in.** Airlines with razor-thin margins cannot afford to guess wrong on a three-year fuel price trajectory. If oil prices drop — say, because of a US-Iran deal or a global recession — carriers locked into ₹115 per litre would be paying a premium over the open market while their competitors who stayed out would benefit from lower prices.

The government has added another complication: international airlines are excluded from the scheme. That means Air India, IndiGo, and other domestic carriers flying international routes may face asymmetric fuel costs compared to foreign competitors operating the same corridors.

**What this means for passengers.** The scheme was designed, in part, to prevent airlines from passing fuel costs directly to passengers through higher fares. But if airlines do not join the scheme, that firewall does not exist. Fares will continue to track fuel costs — and right now, that means they stay elevated.

For NRIs booking flights to India this summer, the calculus is clear: airfares are unlikely to come down soon. Pakistan's airspace closure continues to add costs and flight time to routes between India and Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia. The ATF fund could have provided a floor — but only if airlines participate.

The aviation sector supports roughly 77 lakh (7.7 million) jobs in India, and the government has cited connectivity — both domestic and international — as a core motivation for the fund. But a mechanism that no one uses stabilises nothing.

Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has said the fund is forward-looking and will not compensate oil marketing companies for past under-recoveries. A dedicated monitoring committee will oversee operations. Separate agreements between individual airlines and oil marketing companies will govern participation.

None of which matters until someone signs on the dotted line. For now, India has a billion-dollar stabilisation fund sitting fully loaded, with no one pulling the trigger.

*Sources: Reuters, Ainvest, VisaVerge*
